title: Traps, release and the trapper
summary: What a trap is, how traps are lettered, how a call releases the target in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, and which trap mistakes are a No Bird.

body.html: A trap is the machine that throws targets. Traps can be manual or automatic (the Compak® Sporting rules also name semi-automatic ones). In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the traps of a stand are lettered from left to right, as seen from the stand: A, B, C and so on (the rulebook names A to D). In Compak® Sporting the six traps are A to F, each with a letter panel.
How a call releases the target: through the referee and the trapper, by hand, or by a sonopull; and what happens when it comes too late.
body.heading: Watch the call and the release

body.html: The shooter asks for the target with a call: the rules name “pull” or “ready”, though in practice the words vary. In Sporting™ the referee then gives a sound signal to the trapper, the person who releases the targets. The target must leave within three seconds of that signal.

In Compak® Sporting the target can be released in three ways: by hand, by remote control or by a sonopull. A sonopull is a microphone that hears the shooter's call and releases the target by itself. With release by hand the target leaves 0 to 3 seconds after the call; a sonopull waits a fixed 0.5 seconds. At international “in line” events, where each shooter goes through stations 1 to 5 in turn, only the sonopull is used, with FITASC-approved electronic refereeing and scoring.
A voice release has a microphone at the station. Your own voice can trigger it. On such a stand, stay silent while the shooter is ready: whisper between targets or step back.

Trap mistakes are a No Bird in both disciplines. Examples: a target broken as it is thrown, one from the wrong trap, one thrown without a call, or one released more than three seconds late. In Sporting™ it is also a No Bird if two targets come out from the traps of the same stand when one was expected. In Compak® Sporting it is a No Bird if another machine of the same field throws a target by mistake.

notes.html: Keep the Latin letters of the traps when you translate: the menu and the score sheet use them.
Do not translate the call itself: it is a signal for the machine, not a sentence.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Trap B is throwing lower than in the showing — tell the referee.
phrases.meaning: The machine's trajectory has changed; the shooter should report it before shooting.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: It's voice release here — don't chat on the stand.
phrases.meaning: A microphone releases targets; talking can launch one.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: The trapper was late on that one — that's a no bird.
phrases.meaning: The target left more than three seconds after the call.

key_points.html: Traps: A, B, C… on a Sporting™ stand (the rulebook names A–D), A–F on a Compak field; keep Latin letters.
Sporting™: referee signals the trapper; target within 3 seconds.
Compak® Sporting: manual 0–3 s, remote, or sonopull with a fixed 0.5 s delay.
Late, wrong-trap or uncalled targets are No Birds; a microphone can hear you.

quiz.q: In Sporting™, how long may it take for the target to leave after the referee's signal?
quiz.explain: A target released later than three seconds is a No Bird.

quiz.q: What is the fixed delay of a sonopull in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: It is set by each shooter

quiz.explain: The sonopull must apply a fixed, unchangeable delay of 0.5 seconds.

quiz.q: You are on a stand with voice release and the shooter is ready. What do you do?

options.text: Give the shooter a last tip aloud
Ask the trapper to wait a moment
Repeat the call word for him
Stay silent; whisper only between targets

quiz.explain: Your voice can trigger the microphone and release a target nobody called.
